slots.hero.heading: Care that starts by listening to the whole problem
slots.hero.body: Appointments are long enough to examine, explain and treat in the same visit. You see the same practitioner each time, and you will always be told what the plan is before it starts.
slots.services.heading: What we treat
slots.services.intro: A patient searches for their symptom, not for a treatment name. Write these as the thing that hurts, and say who each one suits.
slots.team.heading: Who you will see
slots.team.intro: Names, registrations and what each of them actually spends the week doing. Replace the placeholder portraits with real photographs before launch.
slots.process.heading: Your first visit
slots.process.intro: Nobody enjoys walking into a room without knowing what happens next. This is the whole of it.
slots.compare.heading: What an appointment costs
slots.compare.intro: The two appointments most patients book, side by side. Replace every figure with your own before this site goes live, and delete a row that does not apply here.
slots.compare.caption: A first appointment and a follow-up compared: how long each takes, what happens, what it costs and what can be claimed back
slots.hours.heading: When we are open
slots.hours.note: The last appointment of the day starts an hour before we close. Ring reception if you need a time outside these hours, because we can sometimes arrange one.
slots.faq.heading: Questions before you book
slots.faq.intro: The ones reception is asked every day. Answer them for your own practice and delete anything that is not true here.
slots.contact.heading: Book an appointment
slots.contact.intro: Ring reception and you will be booked in on the call. Email is fine for anything that is not urgent, and we answer the same day we open.
slots.contact.hours: Monday to Saturday, early and late appointments

services.item.title: Back, neck and shoulder pain
services.item.body: Assessment, hands-on treatment and a plan you can keep up with at home. Most people are seen within a week of ringing.

services.item.title: Injury, and getting back to it
services.item.body: Sport, work or a fall. We rehabilitate towards the thing you actually want to do again, and say honestly how long it takes.

services.item.title: Long-term and recurring conditions
services.item.body: Ongoing care for something that comes back, coordinated with your GP or specialist when that helps.

process.step.title: We talk about what brought you in
process.step.body: History, what makes it worse, what you have already tried, and what you need to be able to do again.

process.step.title: An examination, and an explanation
process.step.body: We assess, then tell you what we think is going on in plain words, including when we are not certain.

process.step.title: Treatment starts the same day
process.step.body: You leave with something done and something to do, and a clear idea of how many visits this is likely to take.

faq.item.question: Do I need a referral?
faq.item.answer: Not to book with us. Say here which arrangements do involve a referral or a care plan in your jurisdiction, and check the wording against the rules that apply to your profession.

faq.item.question: What happens if I have to see somebody else?
faq.item.answer: Say what happens when the practitioner somebody has been seeing is away, and whether their notes go with them. Fees and rebates are in the table above rather than here, so there is one place to keep them up to date.

faq.item.question: How long will I have to wait?
faq.item.answer: Give a real range rather than a comforting one, and say how a cancellation list works if you keep one. A patient who is told three days and waits nine does not come back.

faq.item.question: What if I have to cancel?
faq.item.answer: State the notice period and any fee here, before somebody books rather than after they miss. It is the sentence that decides whether a cancellation policy feels fair.

faq.item.question: Is the practice accessible, and is there parking?
faq.item.answer: Describe the entrance, the stairs or the lift, and the parking honestly. Somebody in pain is deciding whether they can physically get to you, and a vague answer reads as a no.
